title: Certifying Skills for Entry-Level Team Members
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article makes the case for building formal skill-certification levels for new and entry-level team members rather than leaving progress vague. It argues that clear, staged milestones let both managers and employees track growth objectively, reducing relational bias in who gets rewarded. The piece cautions against cutesy or juvenile labels for these levels, since they can invite ridicule from more experienced staff, recommending neutral numbers or letters instead. It closes by suggesting the same certification logic can motivate even tenured employees, not just newcomers.
points: New and entry-level employees want visible proof of their growing skill and reliability, not just praise.
Formal levels or certifications make progress objective and reduce bias in who gets rewarded.
Reaching a new certified level should come with tangible rewards to reinforce the behavior.
Avoid gimmicky labels like gold stars or animal names, which can draw derision from tenured staff.
Numbers or letters work better than cute names for signaling where someone stands.
The same certification approach can also re-motivate experienced team members.
quotes: Even hourly, temporary, and short-term contractors seek validation after they have shown themselves to be an asset to the team.
For managers, the line between rookie and established team member is not always easy to discern.
Creating steps or levels where new team members can showcase their skills can prove highly motivational, as well as clarifying.
By giving more rewards to any new team member when they become certified at the next level, the pride in developing new skills becomes infectious.
Good leaders avoid youthful labels to acknowledge successive levels, such as gold stars, animal names, and hokey comparisons.
A more precise description of skill development motivates everyone to excel, even the more seasoned team members.
